alt: The null hypothesis predicts no difference in names recalled by doodlers and non-doodlers. The alternative hypothesis predicts a difference and comes in two versions: directional (doodlers will recall more) and non-directional (there will be a difference). A note explains when to choose a directional hypothesis.
caption: Null says no difference; directional says which way; non-directional just says different.

alt: The caffeine study's independent variable (200 ml of coffee or decaffeinated coffee 30 minutes before) and dependent variable (target letters crossed out in two minutes). Below, controls: the same time of day, no caffeine beforehand, and a standardised procedure. A note defines confounding.
caption: Define the IV and DV precisely, then hold everything else constant.

alt: Three panels each show a population of 40 dots with 8 picked. Opportunity sampling picks a cluster of whoever is available (quick, but unrepresentative); random sampling picks scattered dots (more representative, needs a full list); volunteer sampling picks those who respond to an advert (easy, but volunteers differ). A note covers generalisation.
caption: Opportunity is quick, random is fairest, volunteers may differ from everyone else.

alt: Dot plots of the invented scores on a 0 to 10 scale. Doodling: 4, 5, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, with mode 5, median 6, mean about 6.3 and range 5. Control: 3, 3, 4, 4, 4, 5, 6, with mode 4, median 4, mean about 4.1 and range 3.
caption: Doodlers scored higher on every average and their scores were more spread out.

alt: Three small graphs: a bar chart with gaps between bars for separate categories, a histogram with no gaps for the frequency of continuous data, and a scatter graph for the relationship between two co-variables. The shapes are illustrative.
caption: Bars with gaps for categories, no gaps for continuous data, points for relationships.
